podcast.title: Dual Meaning of Band Name
podcast.body: The band's name, Kashtin, holds two meanings: it means "tornado" in their native language, and it also serves as a playful response to people back home who thought they were "selling out," with the band retorting, "No, no, no, they said we're cached in." "Their name has two meanings. First of all, it means tornado in their language, but it's also a bit of a joke because some of the people back home thought they were selling out. No, no, no, they said we're cached in."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historical Success for First Nations
podcast.body: Radio play and record sales in their early career helped establish Kashtin as one of the most successful First Nations bands in Canadian history, paving the way for future Indigenous artists. "Radio play and record sales back then helped establish Cache Den as one of the most successful First Nations bands in Canadian history."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Innu Origins
podcast.body: Claude McKenzie and Florent Vollant, the duo forming Kashtin, are Innu men from the Maliotenam Reserve, situated along the St. Lawrence River in Quebec. This region and their heritage are central to their identity and music. "This was Claude McKenzie and Florent Voulotte, two innuemen from the Malio Tenem Reserve, which is along the St. Lawrence River in Quebec."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: International Success
podcast.body: Kashtin released three albums that not only became hits in Quebec but also gained popularity in parts of English Canada, France, and surprisingly, Greenland. This international reach established them as significant First Nations artists. "There were three cached in albums, which not only became hits in Quebec, but also in parts of English, Canada, France, and all places, Greenland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Singing in Innu-aimun
podcast.body: Kashtin sang in the Innu-aimun language, which is spoken by fewer than 12,000 people. Their decision to use their native tongue in their music brought this language to a wider audience. "Cache Den sang in a language known as innuemen, which is spoken by fewer than 12,000 people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
